content: Toxic Oil Syndrome (TOS) was the name given to a peculiar disease outbreak that occurred in Spain in 1981. The initial presentation of the disease resembled a lung infection, but it exhibited unusual characteristics. Despite the symptoms mimicking a respiratory infection, antibiotics proved to be ineffective in treating the condition. The disease appeared to be geographically localized, and it was observed that multiple members of a single family could be affected, while their neighbors remained asymptomatic. After the acute phase of the illness, patients developed a variety of chronic symptoms. The cause of the syndrome was eventually traced to the consumption of rapeseed oil that had been intended for industrial use rather than for human consumption. This oil had been imported as a low-cost industrial product by the company RAPSA in San Sebastián, processed by RAELCA, and refined by ITH in Seville. It was then sold as olive oil by street vendors at weekly markets, leading to its use in cooking and salads. The widely accepted hypothesis is that toxic compounds formed during the refining process, which was used to remove aniline—a chemical used to denature oils intended for industrial purposes. Once the source of the syndrome was identified, public health officials implemented an exchange program. This program allowed individuals who had purchased the contaminated oil to exchange it for pure olive oil, effectively halting the outbreak. The conclusion that the oil was the cause of TOS is supported by robust epidemiological evidence. However, experimental studies conducted on various laboratory animals have failed to replicate the symptoms observed in human cases of TOS. Neither in vivo nor in vitro studies using toxic oil-specific components, such as fatty acid anilides and esters of PAP (phenylamino-propane), have provided conclusive evidence that these markers are causally involved in the pathogenesis of TOS. The involvement of a U.S. military base in Torrejón de Ardoz and the secrecy surrounding the extensive investigations into the outbreak fueled conspiracy theories about the origins and nature of the syndrome.
